To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prospective teachers are somewhat knowledgeable about the brain and neuroscience, but that they believe in neuromyth.
prospective teachers have a good general knowledge about the human brain and that this knowledge is a good safeguard against believing in myths.

although prospective teachers are generally positive about the use of neuroscience findings in the classroom, they are somewhat knowledgeable about the brain and its functions, but are less well informed when comes to special education.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of academic instruction on the brain for prospective teachers, and with its potential for enhancing their knowledge on the brain and their ability to critically assess information about the brain.
the need of academic instruction on the brain and neuroscience in teachers' curricula and the role that this can play in the development of a more evidence-informed educational practice.
how to promote the integration of neuroscience findings into education and how to avoid the proliferation of neuromythology in the classroom.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the more a teacher knows about the brain, the better he/she can avoid falling into neuromyths.
the more knowledge about the brain, the less likely the prevalence of neuromyhs.
the majority of the students in the Departments of education in the two Universities of Greece have a positive attitude towards neuroeducation and they have an average knowledge about the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neuroscience knowledge is not yet a part of the curricula for teachers in Greece, which may lead to an overestimation of the role of the brain in learning and to a proliferation of myths.
there is a need for a systematic effort to improve teachers’ neuroscience knowledge.
the more one knows about the brain the less he believes in neuromyhs and the more critical he is in reading neuroscientific articles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prospective teachers can be good candidates for promoting neuroeducation, as long as they are properly educated on neuroscience and critical thinking.
neuroscience knowledge is a powerful tool in the hands of educators and that teachers should not shy away from it.
prospective teachers should be provided with the opportunity to acquire a solid background knowledge on the brain.
